solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Right to divide Scotsman’s brandy (4)

indicatorNotes.to divide: R splits MAC in two, sitting between MA and C

blocks.note: Mac, the stock crossword Scotsman (from the 'Mac' of Scottish surnames)

annotation.surface: A dram of a Scotsman's brandy being fairly shared out.
annotation.walkthrough: The possessive 's on Scotsman just attaches him to the brandy in the surface; the wordplay reads R dividing MAC.
annotation.definitionFit: Marc is a brandy distilled from the skins and pips left after winemaking.

entries.clue: Champion prop getting in beer (7)

indicatorNotes.getting in: something getting in another enters it, so POST is placed inside ALE

annotation.surface: A champion rugby prop enjoying his beer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Prop' suggests a rugby forward, but here it is a support, a POST; 'champion' is the definition in its sense of an advocate of a cause.
annotation.definitionFit: An apostle of a cause is its champion, a leading supporter.

entries.clue: Limitations of costly confectionery in US (5)

indicatorNotes.Limitations of: the limits of a word are its first and last letters

blocks.note: a word is written in to join the two limits into a phrase

annotation.surface: An observation that American sweets have their price limits.
annotation.walkthrough: The trick is to read the two outer letters as a phrase, 'C and Y', which runs together into the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Candy is the American word for sweets or confectionery.

entries.clue: Hunting dog terribly loud, Ken holding lead in hall (8)

indicatorNotes.terribly: LOUD KEN is rearranged, as if done terribly
indicatorNotes.lead in: the lead of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: first letter of HALL, held after the third letter of the jumble

annotation.surface: A man called Ken is being terribly loud while a hunting dog waits in the hall.
annotation.walkthrough: The dog of the definition is literally in the surface, which helps; the H goes into the middle of the jumbled LOUD KEN.
annotation.definitionFit: An elkhound is a Norwegian hunting dog, bred to track elk.

entries.clue: Meg Ryan regularly ignored age (3)

indicatorNotes.regularly ignored: every other letter is dropped, leaving the ones between

blocks.note: drop the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters (M, G, Y, N) and keep the rest

annotation.surface: A remark that the actress Meg Ryan has been passed over as she got older.
annotation.walkthrough: Regular letters can be the odd ones or the even ones; here the first is dropped, so the even-placed letters survive.
annotation.definitionFit: An era is an age, a long period of history.

entries.clue: Monarch, secretive, joining new knight somewhere in East Anglia (5,4)

annotation.surface: A secretive monarch teams up with a newly made knight somewhere in the east of England.
annotation.walkthrough: The S of KING'S belongs to SLY, so the split between the words of the answer falls in a different place from the wordplay. East Anglia is the region of eastern England covering Norfolk and Suffolk.
annotation.definitionFit: King's Lynn is a port town in Norfolk, in East Anglia.

entries.clue: Character overseas moronic surprisingly (7)

indicatorNotes.surprisingly: the letters of MORONIC turn out in a surprising order

annotation.surface: Someone abroad behaving surprisingly stupidly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' is a letter, and 'overseas' says it belongs to a foreign alphabet, here Greek.
annotation.definitionFit: Omicron is the fifteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, a character used abroad.

entries.clue: Mexican food found in Arizona chophouse (5)

indicatorNotes.found in: the answer is found inside the words that follow

annotation.surface: Mexican food turning up at a steak restaurant in Arizona.
annotation.walkthrough: A chophouse is a restaurant serving chops and steaks; Arizona borders Mexico, so the surface is plausible.
annotation.definitionFit: A nacho is a tortilla chip topped with cheese, a Mexican snack.

entries.clue: Maybe Ben’s horse in top-class condition heading for Newmarket (8)

indicatorNotes.heading for: the heading of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a mount is a horse you ride
A1 = top-class, with the 1 read as the letter I

annotation.surface: A man called Ben has a horse in peak condition heading for the racecourse at Newmarket.
annotation.walkthrough: Ben is not a man but a Scottish word for a mountain, as in Ben Nevis; 'maybe' marks it as an example. Newmarket is the centre of English horse racing.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: ben is the Scots word for a peak, so any Ben is one instance of the answer.

entries.clue: Long letter (eighth) wanting answer (4)

indicatorNotes.wanting: the letter's name is wanting, lacking, A

blocks.note: H is the eighth letter of the alphabet, spelt out as AITCH
A = answer, removed from the front

annotation.surface: Someone waiting for a long letter's eighth page, still without a reply.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Long' is the verb, as in longing for something, not the adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: a restless craving, as in itching to get started.

entries.clue: Live temporarily with American in hovel (4)

indicatorNotes.in: 'with American in hovel' places the American inside the hovel, so A sits within STY

blocks.note: a sty is a filthy hovel

annotation.surface: Lodging for a while with an American in a run-down shack.
annotation.walkthrough: A sty is a pig pen, and by extension any squalid dwelling.
annotation.definitionFit: To stay somewhere is to live there for a short time.

entries.clue: Fungus spread rapidly (8)

blocks.note: the noun sense: a common edible growth
the verb sense: to grow or expand fast

annotation.surface: A mould creeping quickly across a surface.
annotation.walkthrough: The verb sense comes from how quickly these growths spring up overnight.
annotation.definitionFit: Noun and verb from one word: the fungus, and its figurative use for anything that springs up overnight.

entries.clue: Naval soldier grabbing scrap of cloth lifted greasy stuff (9)

indicatorNotes.lifted: in a down clue, lifting a word turns it upside down, so RAG becomes GAR

blocks.note: a marine is a soldier serving with the navy
a rag is a scrap of cloth

annotation.surface: A marine grabbing a rag and lifting some oily muck.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' looks like it means stole, but in a down clue it reverses: RAG read upwards is GAR.
annotation.definitionFit: Margarine is a butter substitute, a greasy spread.

entries.clue: One owing money, say, finally sold single Born to Run (6)

indicatorNotes.finally: take the final letter of each of the next two words

blocks.note: last letters of SOLD and SINGLE
R = run, as in cricket scores

annotation.surface: Someone in debt who finally sold their copy of the Springsteen single Born to Run.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Born to Run' looks like one title but splits into three pieces: B, TO, R. 'Finally' governs both 'sold' and 'single'.
annotation.definitionFit: A debtor is a person who owes money.

entries.clue: Tense, work not as much? Adult model may appear thus (7)

annotation.surface: A tense question about working less, followed by a note on how a glamour model might pose.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like an adjective about stress but is the grammar term, abbreviated T.
annotation.definitionFit: An adult model might pose topless, so 'thus' stands for the answer.

entries.clue: Vigorously jerked part of foot, left unseen, in yard (6)

indicatorNotes.unseen: L drops out of sight, removed from ANKLE
indicatorNotes.in: 'in yard' places what remains inside the yard, so ANKE sits within YD

blocks.note: the ankle joins the foot to the leg
L = left, removed from ANKLE to leave ANKE

annotation.surface: Someone who wrenched part of their foot while out of sight in the yard.
annotation.walkthrough: The ankle is not strictly part of the foot, but setters treat it loosely as such.
annotation.definitionFit: Yanked means pulled with a sudden vigorous jerk.

entries.clue: European Commission man alone uncovered rank in organisation (7)

indicatorNotes.uncovered: ALONE loses its outer letters, its cover

blocks.note: ALONE without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A lone official at the European Commission, exposed within the organisation's hierarchy.
annotation.walkthrough: Setters often use 'uncovered' to strip both outer letters, not just the first.
annotation.definitionFit: Originally a military term for a stepped troop formation, now used for any tier of a hierarchy, as in the upper echelons.

entries.clue: Clergyman’s tea without milk or sugar? (8)

blocks.note: cha (or char) is British slang for tea
tea with nothing added is plain

annotation.surface: A vicar asks for his tea black and unsweetened.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is': Clergyman is CHA + PLAIN. The question mark flags that 'plain' is a loose description of the tea.
annotation.definitionFit: A chaplain is a clergyman attached to a chapel, regiment, school or hospital.

entries.clue: Huge number of people gather in auditorium (5)

indicatorNotes.in auditorium: an auditorium is where things are heard, so the word is taken as heard

blocks.note: to hoard is to gather and store up

annotation.surface: A huge crowd assembling in a concert hall.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a crowd, which is the definition; the auditorium is the sound signal, not the scene.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, first used of nomadic tribes and now of any teeming crowd.

entries.clue: Some hiker hurried over European river (4)

indicatorNotes.Some: only some of the letters are used
indicatorNotes.over: the letters are read back over, right to left

annotation.surface: A walker hurrying across a river in Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like crossing the river, but it is the reversal signal.
annotation.definitionFit: The Ruhr is a river in western Germany that gives its name to the industrial region.

entries.clue: Steal from home bird (5)

blocks.note: to rob is to steal from

annotation.surface: A burglary at a house, or a bird lifting something from home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Steal from home' reads as one phrase about burglary; it breaks after 'from'.
annotation.definitionFit: The robin is a small bird with a red breast.

entries.clue: Lake that is beyond edges of Exmoor (4)

indicatorNotes.edges of: the edges of a word are its first and last letters

blocks.note: first and last letters of EXMOOR

annotation.surface: A lake just past the boundary of Exmoor.
annotation.walkthrough: Exmoor is a national park in south-west England; Lake Erie is far away in North America, so the scene is a decoy.
annotation.definitionFit: Erie is one of the Great Lakes of North America.

entries.clue: One traditional athletics race keeping crowd riveted? (8)

indicatorNotes.keeping: a race keeping a crowd holds it within, so MILE wraps around MOB

blocks.note: the mile is the classic imperial-distance race

annotation.surface: A classic mile race holding the crowd spellbound.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Riveted' in the surface means enthralled; the question mark lets it mean fixed in place, unable to move.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone riveted to the spot is immobile, unable to move.

entries.clue: Mother and daughter out to lunch (3)

annotation.surface: A mother and daughter who have gone out for lunch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Out to lunch' is not a meal but slang for crazy.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who is out to lunch is not all there, i.e. mad.

entries.clue: Absurd debates start to demand support for lying people? (8)

indicatorNotes.Absurd: DEBATES are rearranged into an absurd order
indicatorNotes.start to: the start of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: Absurd debates begin with demands to support liars.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lying people' look like liars, but they are people lying down, in bed.
annotation.definitionFit: A bedstead is the frame of a bed, which supports people lying on it.

entries.clue: Name fashionable English square (4)

annotation.surface: Naming a trendy square in England.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Square' looks like a town square, but it is a square number: nine is three squared.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example from arithmetic: it is three multiplied by itself.
